title: Find Any Local Peak
statement:
You get an integer list nums where no two neighbouring values are equal. A peak is an index whose value is strictly greater than both of its neighbours.

The list's edges count as next to -∞: index 0 only has to beat nums[1], and the last index only has to beat the one before it. A list with one item is a peak by itself.

Return the index of any peak. When there are several, every one of them is accepted.

Your solution must run in O(log n) time.

examples.why: 9 beats 2 and 4, so index 1 is a peak. Index 3 (6 beats 4 and 1) is one too, and returning 3 is just as correct.
The values only rise, so the only peak is the last index: past the edge counts as -∞. A search that never considers the edges finds nothing.
Index 0 beats its only neighbour. Index 2 (4) also beats both of its neighbours. A rule like "the global maximum" works but costs O(n).

hints: Stand at index mid and look at mid + 1. If the next value is bigger, what must happen somewhere to the right?
Walk uphill from mid toward the bigger neighbour. Either the values turn down at some point, which is a peak, or you reach the edge, which is a peak too. So that side surely has one.
Keep [lo, hi] as a range that surely holds a peak. If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], set lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid. When lo === hi, that index is a peak.

explain.intuition:
Binary search usually needs sorted data. Here it needs something weaker: a reason to throw half away. Look at mid and its right neighbour. If nums[mid + 1] is bigger, start walking right while the values keep rising. They either fall at some point, and the top of the climb is a peak, or they rise all the way to the edge, and the last index is a peak because the edge counts as -∞. Either way a peak must exist to the right of mid. If nums[mid] is the bigger one, the same argument walking left says a peak exists at mid or to its left.

So the invariant is "the range [lo, hi] always contains a peak", not "the range is sorted". You are not searching for one specific index. Any index that the invariant leaves at the end is valid, and that is why any peak is accepted.
steps: Set lo = 0, hi = n − 1. Promise: [lo, hi] contains a peak, counting the edges as -∞.
While lo < hi, take mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2). Because it rounds down, mid + 1 <= hi always exists.
If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], the climb to the right holds a peak: lo = mid + 1.
Otherwise nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1], so mid or something to its left is a peak: hi = mid.
pitfalls: Writing while (lo <= hi) with hi = mid. At lo === hi nothing changes and the loop never ends; and when mid is the last index, nums[mid + 1] reads past the end.
Setting hi = mid − 1 when nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1]. mid may be the only peak in range, as in [0, 10, 0].
Comparing mid with mid − 1 and rounding down. With two items left, mid === lo and mid − 1 is outside the range. If you prefer to look left, round mid up.

solutions.title: Walk until the values fall
solutions.idea: Index i is a peak as soon as nums[i] > nums[i + 1], since you only got there by rising. If that never happens, the last index is the peak.

solutions.title: Binary search toward the higher neighbour
solutions.idea: The side of mid with the bigger neighbour always holds a peak, because a climb must end in a fall or at an edge. Keep that side.

followups: Neighbouring values may now be equal. Does the argument still hold? Try [1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1].
